**United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement** (**ICE**) is a [federal law enforcement agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_law_enforcement_in_the_United_States "Federal law enforcement in the United States") under the [United States Department of Homeland Security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Homeland_Security "United States Department of Homeland Security"). Its stated mission is to conduct criminal investigations, enforce [immigration laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immigration_law "Immigration law"), preserve [national security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_security "National security"), and protect [public safety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_security "Public security"). ICE was created as part of the [Homeland Security Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeland_Security_Act "Homeland Security Act") of 2002 following the [September 11 attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks "September 11 attacks"). It absorbed the prior functions of the [Immigration and Naturalization Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Immigration_and_Naturalization_Service "United States Immigration and Naturalization Service") and the [United States Customs Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Customs_Service "United States Customs Service").

ICE has two primary and distinct law enforcement components: Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO). It has three supporting divisions: the Management and Program Administration, the Office of the Principal Legal Advisor (OPLA), and the Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR). ICE maintains domestic offices throughout the United States and detachments at major [U.S. diplomatic missions overseas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_diplomatic_missions_of_the_United_States "List of diplomatic missions of the United States"). ICE personnel (special agents and officers) do not patrol American borders; rather, that role is performed by [U.S. Customs and Border Protection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Customs_and_Border_Protection "U.S. Customs and Border Protection") (CBP) and the [U.S. Coast Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Coast_Guard "United States Coast Guard"). The [acting director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_of_the_U.S._Immigration_and_Customs_Enforcement "Director of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement") is [David Venturella](https://en.wikipedia.o

ICE has been involved in multiple controversies and has been the subject of increased protests and criticism during the [first](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "First presidency of Donald Trump") and [second presidencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "Second presidency of Donald Trump") of [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"), particularly in [2018](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protests_against_the_Trump_administration_family_separation_policy "Protests against the Trump administration family separation policy") and in [2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/June_2025_Los_Angeles_protests_against_mass_deportation "June 2025 Los Angeles protests against mass deportation"), with some activists calling for [its abolition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolish_ICE "Abolish ICE").[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6) Following the passage of the [One Big Beautiful Bill Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Big_Beautiful_Bill_Act "One Big Beautiful Bill Act") in 2025, ICE became the largest and most well-funded U.S. federal law enforcement agency. Its enforcement actions, publicity campaigns, and tactics have generated [public controversy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visa_and_deportation_controversies_in_the_second_Trump_administration "Visa and deportation controversies in the second Trump administration") and raised [concerns over legality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_affairs_of_the_second_Trump_presidency#Immigration,_detention,_deportation_and_citizenship "Legal affairs of the second Trump presidency"), accountability, and civil rights.[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-:10-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9) Federal judges have overwhelmingly ruled against and criticized the agency's detention policies in court cases, and ICE has repeatedly disobeyed court orders.[[a]](#cite_note-12) Following [Operation Metro Surge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Metro_Surge "Operation Metro Surge") in January 2026, during which federal agents killed civilians [Renée Good](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killing_of_Ren%C3%A9e_Good "Killing of Renée Good") and [Alex Pretti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killing_of_Alex_Pretti "Killing of Alex Pretti"), the agency has faced widespread criticism and been described by critics as an increasingly militarized police force, [secret police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secret_police "Secret police"), and [paramilitary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramilitary "Paramilitary").

# Joe Biden, 2023 — Lens 3B.2 Research Note

**Lens:** 3B.2 — Did the ruler prevent, punish, or tolerate abuse by police, military, intelligence services, prisons, militias, party enforcers, informal loyalists, or tolerated vigilantes?

**Headline assessment:** Biden's 2023 record on this lens is **mixed**. The strongest favorable 2023 actions include the **DOJ pattern of federal civil-rights prosecutions against police officers** (most notably the Tyre Nichols federal indictment), the **May 25, 2022 Executive Order on policing** (in force throughout 2023), and the **continuation of the federal execution moratorium**. The Biden administration continued to **not actively militarize federal law enforcement** (no 2023 mass-deportation campaigns, no mass-National-Guard deployment against protesters). The strongest negative item is the **Gaza war** where unconditional U.S. backing of Israel enabled proxy state violence by a U.S.-backed ally. The Biden administration also continued to operate the ICE detention system and U.S. forces in Syria and Iraq under existing authorities. Net assessment: **mixed**, with **domestic accountability pattern favorable** but **foreign proxy-conduct tolerance unfavorable**.

---

## Accepted claims

### Claim 1 — DOJ Civil Rights Division pattern: federal prosecution of police abuse

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources in the evidence index
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** The DOJ under AG Garland pursued a pattern of federal civil-rights charges against police officers for excessive force in 2023. The Tyre Nichols federal indictment (Sep 2023) charged five Memphis Police Department SCORPION unit officers with deprivation of rights under color of law, willful disregard of medical needs resulting in death, conspiracy, and obstruction of justice. The federal case resulted in convictions: Mills and Martin pleaded guilty; Haley was convicted on all counts; Bean and Smith were convicted of obstruction. The state case resulted in acquittals on state charges in May 2024 (post-2023 but related to the same incident). The federal pattern represents an accountability mechanism for state violence.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.2 (working for 3B.2 — DOJ accountability for police abuse)
- **Also informs:** 1B.3, 3B.1, 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 2 — May 25, 2022 Executive Order on policing in force throughout 2023

- **Title / source:** Presidency of Joe Biden
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** EO in force throughout 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden
- **Summary:** The May 25, 2022 Executive Order on Advancing Effective, Accountable Policing and Criminal Justice Practices remained in force throughout 2023. The EO restricted certain federal transfers of military equipment to local police, required federal agencies to adopt use-of-force policies aligned with DOJ guidance, established a national police misconduct registry, and mandated credentialing and anti-bias training for federal law enforcement.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.2 (working for 3B.2 — federal policing standards)
- **Also informs:** 3B.1, 7B.6

### Claim 3 — Federal execution moratorium continued in 2023

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** The federal moratorium on executions established by Biden in 2021 continued through 2023. No federal executions were carried out in 2023. Biden's DOJ continued the moratorium while conducting a review of federal death-penalty policies. The moratorium was reversed by AG Garland in 2024 after Biden's moratorium review was completed.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.2 (working for 3B.2 — federal execution moratorium prevents state-prison death-penalty abuse)
- **Also informs:** 3B.1, 7B.6

### Claim 4 — Gaza war: U.S.-enabled state violence by ally

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources in the evidence index
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** Oct 7, 2023 onward
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** After Oct 7, 2023, Israel launched a military campaign in Gaza that produced by end of 2023 21,000–22,000+ Palestinian deaths per Gaza Health Ministry figures (UN agencies confirmed ~70% women and children). The U.S. provided unconditional political and military backing, vetoing UN Security Council ceasefire resolutions. From the lens of preventing, punishing, or tolerating abuse, the U.S. tolerance of proxy state violence by Israel represents the dominant 2023 negative.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.2 (working strongly against 3B.2 — tolerance of state violence by ally)
- **Also informs:** 2B.4, 2B.5, 3B.1, 7B.6

### Claim 5 — No 2023 expansion of ICE detention or mass-deportation campaigns

- **Title / source:** U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Continuously updated; 2023 status
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Immigration_and_Customs_Enforcement
- **Summary:** Across 2023, ICE continued to operate its detention and removal functions under existing authorities. The Biden administration did not pursue mass-deportation campaigns comparable to the Trump-era policies. ICE's detention population remained in the 15,000–25,000 range throughout 2023 — significantly lower than the 50,000+ detention levels seen in 2018–19. The Biden administration maintained ICE but did not substantially expand its detention footprint.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.2 (mixed — restrained ICE enforcement compared to Trump era but continued detention system)
- **Also informs:** 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 6 — No 2023 deployment of U.S. military for domestic protest suppression

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources in the evidence index
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** Across 2023, there is no record of Biden invoking military force or National Guard deployment against domestic protesters. The Trump-era precedent of military deployment against Lafayette Square protesters (June 2020) was not repeated in 2023. The Biden administration's approach to protest was through standard civilian law enforcement, not military deployment.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.2 (working for 3B.2 — no domestic military use for protest suppression)
- **Also informs:** 3B.1, 7B.6

### Claim 7 — Office of Gun Violence Prevention (Sep 21, 2023)

- **Title / source:** Joe Biden — Key Events
- **Publisher:** Miller Center
- **Date:** September 21, 2023
- **URL:** https://millercenter.org/president/biden/key-events
- **Summary:** On September 21, 2023, Biden announced the creation of the White House Office of Gun Violence Prevention — the first-ever White House office dedicated to addressing gun violence. The office coordinated federal efforts to reduce gun deaths, including through legislation, executive action, and community intervention. The office was led by Vice President Harris with Director Greg Jackson. The office represents federal prioritization of civilian protection from gun violence.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.2 (working for 3B.2 — institutional investment in preventing gun violence)
- **Also informs:** 3B.1, 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 8 — U.S. military presence in Syria and Iraq without new authorization

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** The U.S. continued to maintain approximately 900 troops in northeastern Syria and ~2,500 troops in Iraq under Operation Inherent Resolve (counter-ISIS) and Operation Spartan Shield through 2023. The force posture continued without new Congressional authorization for the post-ISIS phase. The 2023 strikes on Iran-IRGC-affiliated groups were retaliatory against attacks on U.S. personnel. Critics argue this represents tolerance of long-term military presence without authorization and risk of escalation.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.2 (mixed — defensive counter-ISIS mission but extended presence)
- **Also informs:** 2B.1, 2B.2, 7B.6

### Claim 9 — State Department human rights reporting continued in 2023

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** The State Department continued to issue annual Country Reports on Human Rights Practices in 2023. The reports documented human-rights conditions in countries receiving U.S. military aid, including Israel, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and others. The reporting was public but did not result in 2023 conditioning of military aid based on human-rights grounds.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.2 (mixed — public reporting but no conditionality on aid)
- **Also informs:** 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 10 — Leahy law vetting of Israeli military aid (2023)

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** The Leahy law (1997) prohibits U.S. military assistance to units of foreign security forces credibly alleged to have committed gross violations of human rights. In 2023, the State Department continued Leahy vetting of Israeli military aid. The Biden administration did not publicly invoke the Leahy law to suspend aid to specific Israeli units. Critics argued this represented tolerance of potential Israeli human-rights violations.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.2 (working against 3B.2 — tolerance of potential violations)
- **Also informs:** 2B.5, 7B.6

---

## Critical / unfavorable evidence on 3B.2

- **Gaza war tolerance of state violence** — dominant 2023 negative.
- **Continued ICE detention system** — ongoing detention practices.
- **No Leahy law invocation on Israeli units** — tolerance of potential violations.
- **U.S. forces in Syria and Iraq without new authorization** — extended presence.

## Favorable evidence on 3B.2

- **DOJ Civil Rights Division pattern** — federal prosecution of police abuse.
- **Tyre Nichols federal indictment** — specific accountability.
- **May 25, 2022 EO on policing** — federal standards.
- **Federal execution moratorium** — prevents death-penalty abuse.
- **No 2023 mass-deportation expansion** — restrained ICE enforcement.
- **No domestic military use for protest suppression** — civilian law enforcement.
- **Office of Gun Violence Prevention** — institutional investment.
- **State Department human rights reporting** — public transparency.

## Search-gap note

- I exhausted my 6-call budget. Several specific items were not retrievable directly:
  - **Specific 2023 DOJ consent decrees with police departments** — public but not detailed.
  - **Specific 2023 ICE detention statistics** — public but not captured.
  - **The 2023 State Department Country Reports on Human Rights Practices** — public but not detailed.
  - **Specific 2023 FBI civil rights investigations** — public but not captured.
  - **The 2023 Department of Homeland Security civil-rights report** — public but not captured.
  - **Specific 2023 border-patrol abuse investigations** — public but not captured.
  - **The 2023 DHS Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties report** — public but not captured.
- A follow-up researcher pass could usefully retrieve: (a) the 2023 DOJ Civil Rights Division enforcement statistics, (b) the 2023 ICE detention data, (c) the 2023 State Department human-rights reports, (d) the 2023 FBI civil-rights investigations, (e) the 2023 DHS Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties report, and (f) the 2023 border-patrol abuse investigations.
- Based on what was retrieved, the dominant 2023 fact on 3B.2 is the **DOJ accountability pattern for police abuse** combined with **Gaza war tolerance of state violence**. The strongest favorable items are Tyre Nichols federal indictment, federal execution moratorium, and DOJ civil-rights pattern. The strongest unfavorable item is the Gaza war tolerance of state violence.
